title: Build queries for Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL

questions.q: Which Cosmos DB resource is the fundamental unit of scalability and holds the JSON items?

options.text: Account
options.why: The account is the top-level management unit with the endpoint.

options.text: Partition key
options.why: A partition key is a container setting, not a resource.

options.text: Database
options.why: A database is a logical namespace that groups containers.

options.text: Container
options.why: Correct. Containers are the unit of scalability and hold items.

questions.hint: Which level of the hierarchy holds the items and is the unit of scale?
questions.explain: Account → database → container → item; containers scale and hold the documents.

questions.q: A chat app stores each user's conversation history. Queries almost always filter by user. Which property is the best partition key?

options.text: /createdDate
options.why: Date keys can create hot partitions during busy periods.

options.text: /isActive
options.why: A boolean gives two partitions and hot spots.

options.text: /userId
options.why: Correct. userId has high cardinality and groups each user's data together.

options.text: /messageType
options.why: A few message types give low cardinality.

questions.hint: Pick a property every item has, with many distinct values, that most queries filter on.
questions.explain: Choose a property that exists in every item, has many distinct values, and matches your queries.

questions.q: Autoscale throughput is configured with a maximum of 4,000 RU/s. What range does the container scale within?

options.why: Correct. Autoscale scales between 10% of the maximum and the maximum.
1,000 RU/s is the smallest allowed maximum, not the floor here.

options.text: 0 to 4,000 RU/s
options.why: Autoscale doesn't go to zero.
The configured value is the maximum.

questions.hint: Autoscale's minimum is a fixed percentage of the maximum you set.
questions.explain: Autoscale minimum = 10% of the configured maximum.

questions.q: Four containers in one database have unpredictable, uneven usage, and the team wants to keep cost down. Where should throughput be provisioned?

options.text: Shared throughput at the database level
options.why: Correct. Database-level throughput is shared across containers with variable usage.

options.text: Dedicated throughput on the busiest container, none on the rest
options.why: The other containers would then have no throughput.

options.text: Dedicated manual throughput on each container
options.why: Dedicated throughput gives predictable performance but costs more for variable usage.

options.text: Autoscale on the account
options.why: Throughput is provisioned on databases or containers, not accounts.

questions.hint: Uneven, unpredictable use across several containers suggests pooling the RUs.
questions.explain: Shared database throughput suits containers with variable usage; dedicated suits critical predictable workloads.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A container uses `/categoryId` as its partition key.

rows.text: Two items can share the id product-1 if they have different categoryId values.
rows.why: id plus partition key value uniquely identifies an item.

rows.text: You can switch the partition key to /brandId later with a setting change.
rows.why: You can't change the partition key without a new container and migration.

rows.text: If you create an item without an id, the SDK generates one for you.
rows.why: You must provide an id; the SDK doesn't generate one.

rows.text: _ts records when the item was last modified, in Unix seconds.
rows.why: _ts is a Unix timestamp of the last modification.

questions.hint: Uniqueness is id plus partition key. The partition key can't change, and the SDK won't invent an id.
questions.explain: Design ids and partition keys up front: the key is permanent and ids are yours to supply.

questions.q: Two workers read the same cached model output, change it and write it back, and one worker's change keeps getting lost. Which system property helps prevent this?

options.text: _ts
options.why: _ts shows when it changed but doesn't block a stale write.

options.text: _self
options.why: _self is a URI for addressing the item.

options.text: _rid
options.why: _rid is an internal resource identifier.

options.text: _etag
options.why: Correct. Writing with an _etag condition fails if the item changed since it was read.

questions.hint: Optimistic concurrency uses a value that changes every time the item changes.
questions.explain: _etag enables optimistic concurrency: the update fails with a conflict if someone else changed the item.

questions.q: A team wants to cut RU consumption for a busy workload. Which three factors does Learn say increase RU charges? (Select three.)

options.text: Projecting fewer properties
options.why: Returning fewer properties can lower RU cost.

options.text: Stronger consistency levels such as strong
options.why: Correct. Strong and bounded staleness consume more RUs.

options.text: Using point reads instead of queries
options.why: Point reads are the cheapest way to read one item.

options.text: Larger item sizes
options.why: Correct. Larger documents cost more to read and write.

options.text: Cross-partition queries
options.why: Correct. Spanning partitions costs more than single-partition queries.

questions.hint: Bigger items, stronger guarantees and wider queries all cost more.
questions.explain: Item size, indexing policy, consistency, query complexity and cross-partition fan-out drive RU cost.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. You're explaining the Cosmos DB for NoSQL resource model to a new developer.

rows.text: The hierarchy runs account → database → container → item.
rows.why: Accounts are the top-level unit, then databases, containers and items.

rows.text: The account provides the DNS endpoint `https://<account-name>.documents.azure.com:443/`.
rows.why: SDK connections use the account's endpoint.

rows.text: Items in one container must all follow the same schema.
rows.why: Containers are schema-agnostic, so items can have different structures.

rows.text: By default, an account can hold up to 500 databases and containers combined.
rows.why: That's the default limit Learn gives.

questions.hint: Think top-down from the account, and remember Cosmos DB doesn't enforce a schema.
questions.explain: Cosmos DB organizes resources as account → database → container → item. The account gives the DNS endpoint; containers are schema-agnostic; by default an account holds up to 500 databases and containers combined.

questions.q: A developer proposes partitioning an inference-results container by the boolean property isActive, because most queries filter on it. What problem does Learn warn about?

options.text: The container would need a nested path such as /metadata/isActive
options.why: Nested paths are allowed, but they don't fix low cardinality.

options.text: Only two values exist, so traffic and data pile up in hot partitions
options.why: Correct. Low-cardinality keys such as booleans create hot partitions and limit scale.

options.text: Queries filtered on isActive would become cross-partition queries
options.why: Filtering on the partition key routes to one partition. The problem is the lack of spread.

options.text: Boolean properties can't be used as partition key paths
options.why: The issue isn't the data type. It's that there are only two values.

questions.hint: How many distinct values does a boolean have? Think about how the data spreads.
questions.explain: Partition keys need high cardinality. A key with only a few values, such as a boolean, creates hot partitions that get disproportionate traffic and storage.

questions.q: A database uses shared manual throughput. The team plans to add many small containers to it. What does Learn say about this model?

options.text: Shared throughput is available only with autoscale
options.why: Shared throughput works with manual throughput too, as this database shows.

options.text: Shared throughput supports an unlimited number of containers
options.why: Learn gives a limit of 25 containers for shared throughput.

options.text: Each container in the database still needs its own 400 RU/s minimum
options.why: That's dedicated container throughput. Shared throughput pools RUs across containers.

options.text: The database has a minimum of 400 RU/s, shared across up to 25 containers
options.why: Correct. Shared database throughput starts at 400 RU/s and can serve up to 25 containers.

questions.hint: Shared throughput has a minimum RU/s and a maximum number of containers.
questions.explain: With manual throughput, a container with dedicated throughput has a minimum of 400 RU/s. A database with shared throughput also has a 400 RU/s minimum and can share it across up to 25 containers.

questions.q: You want to log how many RUs each Cosmos DB operation in your app uses, so that you can find expensive ones. Where does each operation report its RU charge?

options.text: In the activity ID returned with each request
options.why: The activity ID identifies a request for support. It isn't the charge.

options.text: Only in Azure Monitor, about an hour later
options.why: Each response carries its charge right away. Azure Monitor is for aggregated views.

options.text: In the x-ms-request-charge response header
options.why: Correct. Every operation returns its RU cost in this header.

options.text: In the item's _ts system property
options.why: _ts is the last-modified timestamp, not a cost.

questions.hint: Each response carries its own cost in a header.
questions.explain: Every operation returns its RU charge in the x-ms-request-charge response header. Log it (with the activity ID) to find expensive patterns.

questions.q: An app fetches a 1-KB user profile by id and partition key, and also writes a 1-KB cached result. Roughly how do the two operations compare in RU cost?

options.text: About 100 RUs each, because both use the network
options.why: Point reads are the cheapest operation, at about 1 RU.

options.text: About 10 RUs for the read; about 1 RU for the write
options.why: That's the wrong way round. Writes cost more than point reads.

options.text: Both cost about the same, because the item size is the same
options.why: Writes include indexing overhead, so they cost more than point reads.

options.text: About 1 RU for the read; about 5–10 RUs for the write
options.why: Correct. A 1-KB point read costs about 1 RU, and a 1-KB write about 5–10 RUs.

questions.hint: Point reads are the cheapest operation there is. Writes pay for indexing too.
questions.explain: Point reads (single 1-KB item by id and partition key) cost around 1 RU. Writing a 1-KB item costs about 5–10 RUs depending on consistency and indexing.

questions.q: A FastAPI service creates a new CosmosClient for every incoming request, and latency is erratic under load. What should you change?

options.text: Create a new client for each container instead of per request
options.why: More clients still discard cached state.

options.text: Create one CosmosClient at startup and reuse it
options.why: Correct. A single reused client keeps warm connection pools and cached routing information.

options.text: Call get_container_client before every query
options.why: Container handles are cheap but don't fix the client problem.

options.text: Switch from Entra ID to account keys
options.why: Authentication method doesn't fix per-request client creation.

questions.hint: Clients hold connection pools and routing caches. How many should an app create?
questions.explain: Register CosmosClient as a singleton or application-scoped service.

questions.q: Which built-in role lets an identity read and write items with Entra ID authentication?

options.text: Cosmos DB Built-in Data Reader
options.why: Data Reader allows read operations only.

options.text: Cosmos DB Account Key Operator
options.why: Learn doesn't list this role.

options.text: Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor
options.why: Correct. Data Contributor allows read and write operations.

options.text: Cosmos DB Built-in Owner
options.why: Learn doesn't list this role.

questions.hint: Read and write with Entra ID: one built-in role says it can contribute data.
questions.explain: Data Reader for reads; Data Contributor for reads and writes.

questions.q: Startup code must make sure the products container exists, and the app may restart many times. Which method should it call?

options.text: database.create_container_if_not_exists()
options.why: Correct. It creates the container if needed and returns it otherwise, so restarts don't fail.

options.text: container.upsert_item()
options.why: upsert_item writes items, not containers.

options.text: database.create_container()
options.why: create_container fails if the container already exists.

options.text: database.get_container_client()
options.why: get_container_client only makes a handle; it doesn't create anything.

questions.hint: Startup code runs many times. Choose the call that's safe to repeat.
questions.explain: *_if_not_exists methods are idempotent, which suits application initialization.

questions.q: Match each SDK call to its behavior.
choices: Fails with 409 if the item exists
Fails if the item doesn't exist
Cheapest way to fetch one known item

items.why: create_item catches accidental duplicates with a 409 Conflict.
upsert creates the item or replaces the existing one.
replace requires the item to exist.

items.text: read_item with id and partition key
items.why: A point read costs about 1 RU for a 1-KB item.

questions.hint: Create fails if it exists, replace fails if it doesn't, and upsert doesn't care.
questions.explain: Pick the write method by whether you expect the item to exist.

questions.q: A cache lookup with read_item raises CosmosResourceNotFoundError when the result hasn't been computed yet. What should the code do?

options.text: Retry read_item until the item appears
options.why: The item doesn't exist yet, so retrying won't help.

options.text: Switch to a cross-partition query to search all partitions
options.why: A query won't find an item that doesn't exist, and it costs more.

options.text: Catch the exception and compute the value as a fallback
options.why: Correct. Handle the exception to compute an uncached value or return a default.

options.text: Recreate the container with create_container_if_not_exists
options.why: The container exists; the item is just missing.

questions.hint: Not found is an expected result for a cache miss. Handle it and compute the value.
questions.explain: Point reads raise CosmosResourceNotFoundError for missing items; use it for fallback logic.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. An app uses an account key in its CosmosClient.

rows.text: Anyone holding that key has full access to all resources in the account.
rows.why: Account keys grant full access to everything in the account.

rows.text: Account keys support conditional access policies from Entra ID.
rows.why: Keys don't integrate with centralized identity management or conditional access.

rows.text: The primary and secondary keys let you rotate a key without downtime.
rows.why: Two keys allow rotation without downtime.

rows.text: get_container_client confirms that the container exists by calling the service.
rows.why: These methods make no network calls and don't verify existence.

questions.hint: An account key is full access to everything, and Entra ID features don't apply to it.
questions.explain: Keys are simple but all-powerful; Entra ID with RBAC is preferred for production.

questions.q: The same FastAPI code must authenticate to Cosmos DB with your Azure CLI login on your laptop and with a managed identity in Azure, with no code change. What should you use?

options.text: DefaultAzureCredential
options.why: Correct. It picks the right credential for the environment: developer sign-in locally, managed identity in Azure.

options.text: A connection string per environment in local.settings.json
options.why: That still uses keys and different values per environment.

options.text: ManagedIdentityCredential only
options.why: A managed identity doesn't exist on your laptop, so local runs would fail.

options.text: The account's primary key from an environment variable
options.why: That's key-based access, which skips Entra ID and RBAC.

questions.hint: One credential class tries several sign-in methods in order.
questions.explain: DefaultAzureCredential selects the credential for the environment: Azure CLI or Visual Studio sign-in locally, managed identity when deployed.

questions.q: A reporting service must read items with Entra ID authentication and must not be able to write. Which built-in role should its identity get?

options.text: Cosmos DB Built-in Data Reader
options.why: Correct. It allows read operations only.

options.text: Owner on the resource group
options.why: Owner is far too broad for reading items.

options.text: Cosmos DB Account Reader Role
options.why: That's a control-plane role for reading account settings, not item data.

options.text: Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor
options.why: Contributor allows reads and writes, which is more than this service needs.

questions.hint: Grant only what's needed: data access, read-only.
questions.explain: The built-in data roles include Cosmos DB Built-in Data Reader for read operations and Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor for read/write.

questions.q: A few writes have unusually high latency, and you plan to open a support case. Besides the RU charge, which value should your code log so that Microsoft support can find each request?

options.text: The item's _etag
options.why: The etag tracks item versions for concurrency, not individual requests.

options.text: The partition key value
options.why: The key routes data. It doesn't identify one request.

options.text: The client's process ID
options.why: Support can't map a local process ID to a service request.

options.text: The activity ID from the response
options.why: Correct. The activity ID uniquely identifies each request, which helps support diagnose it.

questions.hint: Each request gets a unique identifier in the response metadata.
questions.explain: Log the activity ID alongside errors or high RU charges. It uniquely identifies each request when working with Azure support.

questions.q: You need a plain JSON array of product names, such as ["Smart Speaker", "Laptop"], without wrapping objects. Which query should you use?

options.text: SELECT COUNT(p.name) FROM products p
options.why: This returns a count, not the names.

options.text: SELECT VALUE p.name FROM products p
options.why: Correct. VALUE returns the scalar values without the surrounding object.

options.text: SELECT * FROM products p
options.why: This returns whole documents.

options.text: SELECT p.name FROM products p
options.why: This returns objects such as {"name": "…"}.

questions.hint: One keyword returns the bare values instead of objects.
questions.explain: SELECT VALUE unwraps results into scalars or custom shapes.

questions.q: A search box sends a category typed by users into a query. How should you build the query?

options.text: Concatenate the user's text into the WHERE clause
options.why: Concatenating user input invites injection.

options.text: Use a parameter such as @category with a parameters array
options.why: Correct. Parameters prevent injection and allow query plan caching.

options.text: Run the query as a stored procedure with the user's text inline
options.why: Inline user text is still unsafe.

options.text: Wrap the user's text in UPPER() before concatenating it
options.why: UPPER changes case but doesn't stop injection.

questions.hint: User input never goes into the query text itself.
questions.explain: Always parameterize values that come from users or external sources.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. The products container is partitioned by `/categoryId`.

rows.text: A query that filters on categoryId = @category can be routed to a single partition.
rows.why: Including the partition key routes the query directly.

rows.text: A query that filters only on price needs enable_cross_partition_query=True.
rows.why: Without the partition key, the query fans out across partitions.

rows.text: WHERE p.name = "speaker" matches an item named "Speaker".
rows.why: String comparisons are case-sensitive by default.

questions.hint: Filtering on the partition key routes to one partition. String comparison is case-sensitive.
questions.explain: Design queries to include the partition key; remember case-sensitive string comparisons.

questions.q: Each product has a features array. You need one result row per matching feature, only for features "wifi" or "bluetooth". Which query does this?

options.text: SELECT p.name FROM products p WHERE CONTAINS(p.features, "wifi")
options.why: CONTAINS is a string function, not an array membership test.

options.text: SELECT p.name FROM products p WHERE ARRAY_CONTAINS(p.features, "wifi") OR ARRAY_CONTAINS(p.features, "bluetooth")
options.why: ARRAY_CONTAINS returns each matching product once; it doesn't flatten the array into one row per feature.

options.text: SELECT p.name, f AS feature FROM products p JOIN f IN p.features WHERE f IN ("wifi", "bluetooth")
options.why: Correct. JOIN … IN flattens the array so you can filter and return individual elements.

options.text: SELECT VALUE p.features FROM products p WHERE p.features = "wifi"
options.why: Comparing an array to a string doesn't test membership.

questions.hint: To get one row per array element, the query has to iterate over the array itself.
questions.explain: Use ARRAY_CONTAINS for membership; JOIN with IN to flatten arrays and filter elements.

questions.q: A dashboard query costs hundreds of RUs. Which two changes match Learn's cost optimization list? (Select two.)

options.text: Remove all WHERE filters and filter in the app
options.why: Filtering early reduces cost; moving filters to the app does the opposite.

options.text: Project only the properties the dashboard shows
options.why: Correct. Returning only needed fields reduces cost.

options.text: Add the partition key to the filter where possible
options.why: Correct. Single-partition routing costs less than fan-out.

options.text: Add ORDER BY to every query to speed it up
options.why: Sorting adds overhead rather than reducing it.

questions.hint: Use the partition key in filters and return only the fields you need.
questions.explain: Filter early, project needed fields, use partition keys, limit with TOP, and tune indexes.

questions.q: Besides preventing injection, why does Learn say a frequently run query should use @parameters instead of building a new query string for each value?

options.text: Parameters make every query single-partition automatically
options.why: Routing depends on the partition key filter, not on parameters.

options.text: Parameters convert the query into a stored procedure
options.why: The query stays a query. Nothing is converted.

options.text: Cosmos DB can cache and reuse the query plan for different values
options.why: Correct. Parameterized queries allow query plan caching, which improves performance for repeated queries.

options.text: Parameters halve the RU charge of the query
options.why: Learn doesn't make that claim. The benefit is plan reuse.

questions.hint: The query text stays the same while the values change. What work can the service skip the next time?
questions.explain: Parameterized queries separate structure from values, preventing injection and letting Cosmos DB cache and reuse query plans for repeated queries with different values.

questions.q: A web API returns search results 50 at a time and lets the client ask for the next page later. How should it implement paging with the SDK?

options.text: Run SELECT * and slice the full result list in memory
options.why: That reads every result on every call, which wastes RUs and memory.

options.text: Store each page in a new container for the client to read
options.why: That adds writes and storage for no benefit.

options.text: Set max_item_count to 50 and return the continuation token to the client
options.why: Correct. The iterator pages with continuation tokens, and max_item_count sets the page size.

options.text: Use OFFSET with the client's page number on each call
options.why: Learn's paging guidance is continuation tokens, which keep query state between pages.

questions.hint: The SDK pages for you. One setting sets the page size, and one value lets you resume.
questions.explain: The SDK's query iterator pages through continuation tokens. Set max_item_count for page size, and return the continuation token so clients can request the next page.
